&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;TL;DR: &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/autoshelf-file-organizer/id6762361021?mt=12"&gt;AutoShelf&lt;/a&gt; ($19.99 one-time) ships an embedded MCP server that works, but do you actually need that? An AI model can write a launchd LaunchAgent and a shell script once and it runs forever, no app, no daemon, no purchase. The MCP's real value only shows up once you're managing enough rules to want conversational audit and editing instead of hand-maintained scripts, and even there, my hands-on testing found the rule engine underneath thin: no dynamic subfolder sorting, limited management by file size, and an action list a fraction of Hazel's. AutoShelf delivers less using AI than its marketing promises and loses the file-organizer argument outright.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;AutoShelf&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I've had a &lt;a href="https://www.noodlesoft.com/"&gt;Hazel&lt;/a&gt; rule watching my Downloads folder since before I can accurately date it. It reads PDF invoices and files them by vendor, decompresses ZIPs and moves the app inside to Applications, converts HEICs to JPG, and hands ebooks to Calibre and audiobooks to Audiobookshelf without me touching any of it. That's the bar. A new license for Hazel is $42, which is steep for some and I've written before &lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/affordable-alternatives-to-hazel"&gt;about cheaper options&lt;/a&gt;. AutoShelf wants to be added to that list, and it's making its case with a feature none of those alternatives had: an MCP server for use with AI agents plus a CLI.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;More Than Just Simple File Management&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;An MCP server built into the app binary&lt;/strong&gt;, not a plugin bolted on after the fact. Point Claude Desktop, Cursor, Codex, or Windsurf at it and describe a rule in plain English instead of building it in a UI.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;A companion CLI&lt;/strong&gt; for scripting rule creation and running jobs from the terminal, the same engine the MCP server talks to.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Where-from metadata as a condition&lt;/strong&gt;, so a rule can act on which browser or app downloaded a file, not just its type or name.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;OCR and Live Text matching&lt;/strong&gt; as of version 2.2, so a rule can file a scanned invoice by what's written on it. Not new ground: Hazel's &lt;code&gt;Contents&lt;/code&gt; attribute has done on-the-fly text recognition on images and text-layer-less PDFs for years, it's the mechanism behind the vendor-filing rule in the intro. AutoShelf catching up to a feature Hazel already had is parity, not an edge.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Multi-action, chainable rules&lt;/strong&gt;: move, tag, rename, and archive to ZIP in a single pass, added in the 2.0 rewrite.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Is It Better Than Hazel for Working With AI?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Does anyone even need a layer between a prompt for file management and their file system? For a well-defined one-off job, not really. A capable AI model can write a launchd LaunchAgent with a &lt;code&gt;WatchPaths&lt;/code&gt; key, native FSEvents, no polling loop, and a small shell script that switches on extension and moves the file. Write it once and it runs forever: no app, no background daemon, no $19.99. That's possible without Hazel or AutoShelf.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An MCP connection can do something a bespoke script can't: with it running, AutoShelf can immediately edit any rule with natural language, without you having to track down the launchd job and script you created six months ago. I created eight AutoShelf rules and asked Claude to check on them through the MCP connection; it returned current rules, current paths, and current enabled/disabled flags. A launchd script has no equivalent self-report; ask it "what are you doing" six months from now and the honest answer is "go read the shell and simulate it," and any edit needs a &lt;code&gt;launchctl unload&lt;/code&gt;/&lt;code&gt;load&lt;/code&gt; before it's live. MCP matters once you're managing enough rules that you'd rather audit, pause, or edit them by asking than by maintaining scripts by hand, or you want the GUI, activity log, and undo the app provides that a bare launchd job doesn't have unless you build it yourself.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Against Hazel specifically, AutoShelf is still ahead on this one front. Hazel doesn't have an MCP server and doesn't claim to; anything an AI does to a Hazel rule today runs through a general-purpose file-editing layer poking at Hazel's XML underneath, which is fragile and unsupported. So among app-based rule engines with a GUI and an activity log, AutoShelf's MCP integration is real. On my Mac, it was easy to set up and worked as advertised on the first try.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Rule Engine Underneath Doesn't Hold Up&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is where my hands-on testing exposed the weaknesses in AutoShelf. It can't sort a folder of mixed files into subfolders by extension unless you create every destination subfolder yourself first and then write a separate rule for each file type. I had to build five nearly identical rules, "Sort PNG files," "Sort JPG files," "Sort JPEG files," "Sort GIF files," "Sort MD files," each one hand-built with its own hardcoded destination path. Hazel does the same job with a single "Sort into subfolder" action and a pattern; AutoShelf makes you write and maintain N rules for N extensions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Two more gaps from my testing: size conditions only go down to whole megabytes, no decimal places, so you can't write a rule for anything under 1 MB or between whole-MB steps. More importantly, AutoShelf's action list (Move, Copy, Trash, Rename, Add Tag, Archive to ZIP, Optimize, Convert Image/Video/Audio, Photos import) is a fraction of Hazel's, which adds sync, upload, tags, color labels, comments, alias creation, three Music/Photos/TV import targets, and five different scripting hooks (Shortcuts, AppleScript, JavaScript, Automator, shell) on top of pause, notify, and rule-chaining controls.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Recursion Illusion&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;AutoShelf's App Store listing says it will "watch any folder you choose, including nested subfolders," and the 1.5 changelog calls it "Nested Folder Watching." &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/autoshelf-file-organizer/id6762361021?mt=12"&gt;(App Store listing)&lt;/a&gt; But on its own Product Hunt launch, the developer told a commenter directly that watched folders are top-level only, files dropped into a subfolder are not picked up, and true recursion is a tracked feature request, not a shipped one. &lt;a href="https://www.producthunt.com/products/autoshelf"&gt;(Product Hunt)&lt;/a&gt; Read charitably, "nested folder watching" means you can manually add specific subfolders you already know about as additional watch targets, one at a time. That is not the same as what Hazel does, which is recursive: add one "Run rules on folder contents" rule and Hazel will walk into subfolders of subfolders it has never seen, at any depth, applying your existing rules the whole way down. &lt;a href="https://www.noodlesoft.com/manual/hazel/advanced-topics/processing-subfolders/"&gt;(Noodlesoft manual)&lt;/a&gt; That's a real discrepancy between AutoShelf's marketing copy and its confirmed current behavior, and now my own rule list shows the practical cost of it: I'm hand-maintaining what Hazel would do with one rule.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Who This Is For, and Who Should Stay on Hazel&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If your files land flat, one folder, no meaningful variety in file type, and you are considering a $19.99 one-time tool with a working AI hook, AutoShelf's free tier is worth an afternoon. If your needs are more complex, stick with Hazel. My own eight-rule test folder is the case study: if you have more than three or four file types, or anywhere the folder structure has depth, AutoShelf turns into more manual rule-building than the automation it's supposed to replace.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Autoshelf%20Has%20an%20MCP%20Server%20You%20Probably%20Don" t need and the rule engine is weak a review style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>

alt="A graphic with the recommended app stack to avoid data loss if your iCloud account gets locked." decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt; TL;DR:&lt;/strong&gt; Part two of the Apple Account series. Backup apps that pull your iCloud data down to storage you control, email providers that speak IMAP/CalDAV/CardDAV so Apple's own apps keep working without iCloud, ways to buy and track software outside the App Store, and a password manager that isn't Keychain. My own five picks are at the end, along with why you should be testing a restore every quarter.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;Disaster Avoidance Apps&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Yesterday I laid out &lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/all-your-eggs-in-one-basket-the-disaster-scenario"&gt;what happens when Apple closes your account&lt;/a&gt;: your identity if it's an @icloud.com address, your photos and messages, your purchases, your hardware in every practical sense, and a 2023 federal ruling that says suspicion is the only standard Apple has to meet. That post was the bad news.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is the other half. These are the apps and services that move your data out from under a single Apple Account, what each one actually protects, and where each one falls short. There are more options here than anyone needs, and I have not run most of them. At the end I'll tell you the five I actually use and why I stopped looking after those.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;iCloud Backup Apps&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;BackiGo.&lt;/strong&gt; Photos, videos, iCloud Drive and Contacts, backed up and restored to USB, NAS, or cloud storage you control. Drive versioning, scheduling, incremental backups, optional client-side encryption, and browsable restoration. I reviewed it here: &lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/backigo-is-a-dependable-full-featured-icloud-backup-solution"&gt;BackiGo is a Dependable and Full Featured iCloud Backup Solution&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Parachute Backup.&lt;/strong&gt; Downloads iCloud Photos and iCloud Drive to external drives, NAS, or cloud folders. Handles originals, edits, Live Photos and Shared Albums, with scheduling and full, incremental or mirror modes. My review: &lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/parachute-backup-specially-designed-for-icloud-and-photos"&gt;Parachute Backup, Specially Designed for iCloud and Photos&lt;/a&gt;. Restore to a location that doesn't depend on the same Apple Account, or you've built a circle. The original dev sold the app and I moved to Backigo.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Time Machine&lt;/strong&gt;, with one warning that undoes the whole thing if you miss it. Turn off Optimize Mac Storage in your iCloud settings. Leave it on and macOS keeps only stubs of your iCloud files locally, so Time Machine dutifully backs up the stubs and you find out the day you need the originals.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;Standards-Based Providers for Email, Calendars and Contacts&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can keep using Apple's Mail, Calendar and Contacts without tying any of the data to your Apple Account, by pointing them at a provider that supports IMAP, CardDAV and CalDAV. Reminders is the exception; Apple moved it to a private format, though Things 3 &lt;a href="https://culturedcode.com/things/support/articles/2803561/"&gt;can pull to-dos out of a designated Reminders list&lt;/a&gt; into its own inbox.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Five providers with full IMAP/CardDAV/CalDAV support on macOS:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.fastmail.com/"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Fastmail&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. JMAP, IMAP, CardDAV and CalDAV, with push sync on Apple devices. Custom domains and third-party app access both come with the Individual plan; the cheaper Basic business plan has neither, so don't buy that one for this purpose. I've been using Fastmail for two years, and it also runs an MCP server if you want your mail reachable from an AI agent.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.mailfence.com/"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Mailfence&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. IMAP, CalDAV and CardDAV syncing straight into Apple Mail and Calendar. Belgium-based, EU jurisdiction.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://posteo.de/"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Posteo&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. IMAP, POP, CalDAV and CardDAV for €1 a month, which makes it the cheapest option on this list by a wide margin. Germany-based with serious privacy protections. It does not support custom domains, so it solves the provider problem without solving the address-ownership problem.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://mailbox.org/"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Mailbox.org&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. CalDAV and CardDAV plus ActiveSync, with a bundled office suite. Germany-based, 30-day free trial.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://runbox.com/"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Runbox&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. IMAP with CalDAV and CardDAV. The Runbox 7 web interface is still in development, so plan on using it through standard clients.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;p&gt;All five work natively with macOS Calendar and Contacts. Fastmail has the smoothest CalDAV experience of the ones I've touched. Posteo is the cheapest. Mailfence leans hardest on open standards.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;Software Acquisition and Licensing&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Whenever you have the choice, download applications directly from the developer rather than from the App Store, so your access survives your Apple Account. You give up automatic updates, Family Sharing, and in a few cases unlimited installs.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Updaters that close the first gap:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://updatest.app/"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Updatest&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. Menu bar updater that scans each app's own metadata to find its update source, covering Homebrew, Mac App Store, Sparkle, Electron and GitHub Releases. $12.99 one-time for 3 Macs, $24.99 for 10. Fourteen-day trial, 30-day money-back guarantee. Requires macOS 15 or later.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://nektony.com/"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Nektony App Cleaner &amp;amp; Uninstaller&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. Broad app coverage with direct update installation, and it handles uninstalls too. $24.95 a year. It's fast and doesn't miss much - but that subscription...&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://max.codes/latest/"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Latest&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. Free and lightweight. Checks Mac App Store and Sparkle apps only, so expect it to catch a fraction of what the paid tools track. It's free, but it misses things the paid apps pick up.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.jibapps.com/apps/trashme3/"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;TrashMe 3&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. Cleaner and uninstaller with update detection as a side feature, plus duplicate files and startup item management. $17.99 one-time, 15-day trial.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://brew.sh/"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Homebrew&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt; &lt;strong&gt;with topgrade&lt;/strong&gt;. One terminal command updates Homebrew packages, Mac App Store apps and system tools. Free, broadest coverage, and the only one here that expects you to be comfortable at a prompt. I run this every four hours with launchd.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Then track the licenses somewhere you can export from:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.apptorium.com/license-store"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;License Store&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. Library for keys, license files, invoices and expiration dates, with drag-and-drop app import and export to CSV, JSON or its own .ls format. $7.99 one-time for the current major version, one user, up to five Macs. Requires macOS 26, which rules it out if you haven't moved to Tahoe. It syncs through iCloud, which is the dependency this whole post is about. Treat the sync as convenience between your own Macs and the manual export as the backup. Export to JSON or CSV on a schedule, put the file wherever your other backups live, and import it once to confirm the round trip works before you need it to.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://bundlehunt.com/appvault"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;AppVault&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. The everything option: app snapshots with restore, unified updates across Sparkle, Homebrew, Mac App Store and Electron, a license vault with CSV import, spending tracker, deep uninstall with 14-day quarantine. $21.99 one-time, lifetime license, 3 Macs. I'm currently testing this.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;An Independent Password Manager&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Keep your passwords, recovery codes, server credentials and export encryption passwords outside iCloud Keychain. Then protect the new vault's recovery material somewhere else again, or you've just relocated your single point of failure.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://bitwarden.com/"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Bitwarden&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. Open source, end-to-end encrypted, cross-platform. The free tier covers unlimited passwords on unlimited devices, which is all most people need. Premium is $19.80 a year and adds encrypted file storage and YubiKey support.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://1password.com/"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;1Password&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. $3.99 a month for individuals. Autofill, Watchtower breach alerts, 14-day trial, and the most polished Apple-side experience of the group. I stopped uing this when it went electron.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://keepass.info/"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;KeePass&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. Free, open source, entirely offline, AES-256 by default, extended by community plugins. No sync and no polish; you build both yourself. The right answer if you want zero dependencies and the wrong one if you want it to just work.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Unless I've said otherwise above, the apps in this post come from research rather than daily use. The five below are the exception.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;What I Actually Run&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Five, and the list has been stable long enough that I've stopped shopping.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;BackiGo&lt;/strong&gt; pulls my iCloud Photos and Drive down to local storage on a schedule. It's the only one on this list that gets irreplaceable data out of Apple's custody.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Fastmail&lt;/strong&gt; holds my mail, calendars and contacts on a domain I own, and Apple's own Mail, Calendar and Contacts talk to it over IMAP, CalDAV and CardDAV without knowing the difference. Two years in. If Apple closed my account tomorrow, my address would still work, which was the whole point.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Updatest&lt;/strong&gt; keeps the direct-download side of my Mac current. Buying from developers instead of the App Store costs you automatic updates, and this is what I bought to pay that cost back.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;License Store&lt;/strong&gt; holds the keys and invoices for everything I didn't buy through Apple. The JSON export goes out on a schedule and lands with my other backups, per the caveat above.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Bitwarden&lt;/strong&gt; keeps my passwords and recovery codes out of iCloud Keychain. The free tier does everything I need and I pay for Premium anyway, because a project I depend on this much should get some money from me.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;Test the Restore, Not the Backup&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;None of this counts until you've restored from it. A backup you have never pulled a file out of is not a backup; it's a hypothesis with a progress bar. Once a quarter, pick something you'd hate to lose, a photo from ten years ago, a document with a deadline attached to it, and restore it to a machine that isn't signed in to the account you're insuring against. Open it. Confirm it's the full-resolution original and not a thumbnail, that the metadata came along, that the encryption password you set eighteen months ago still unlocks the archive. The failures I've seen were never missing backups. They were backups that ran green for two years and turned out to be empty, stale, or locked with a password nobody wrote down.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=The%20Apps%20I%20Use%20So%20Apple%20Can" t take everything style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>

&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;TL;DR:&lt;/strong&gt; Mac power users vet apps carefully and then hand their entire digital life to Apple without a second thought. Apple can close your account on suspicion alone, keep your unspent balance, and never tell you why; a federal judge confirmed all of that in 2023 and threw the case out. An Apple Account is simultaneously an authentication system, cloud-storage account, software license repository, device-activation credential, communications identity, and payment account. A full lockout can therefore affect data, purchases, services, and hardware management at once.This post covers how accounts get closed, what you lose when it happens, why getting back in is so hard, and eleven things to do about it now.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;All Your Eggs in One Basket, The Disaster Scenario&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;When the conversation turns to abandoning third party apps in favor of using Apple's default stack, I keep waiting for someone to mention the huge red flag that should instantly discourage making that move without taking some intense protective measures.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The steps I take before adding an app to my workflow are second nature. but detailed. They are probably the same steps most of you take. First I evaluate the feature set to see if it meets my needs. I look at the privacy policy, the cost of buying the app, and the cost of keeping it updated. Any app that takes a significant investment of money or time gets some research about the developer or the company behind it. Sometimes a one-person development team means the app dies when the dev loses interest. Finally I look at what third-party services the app depends on. Dropping $90 on an app Google can kill with an abitrary decsion isn't a deal breaker every time. Just most of the time.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Until last December, I did not apply the same scrutiny to the infrastructure underneath all of it, the company behind much of my digital life. I'm talking about Apple. An entire career in Mac support didn't give me a full understanding of what losing access to an Apple Account would do to someone personally and professionally.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Then Paris Buttfield-Addison, who has written more than twenty books on Apple development and helps put on the longest-running Apple developer conference Apple doesn't run itself, &lt;a href="https://hey.paris/posts/appleid/"&gt;found his account closed&lt;/a&gt; for reasons Apple would not specify. After some of the biggest names in Mac journalism publicized the case, his account was restored, but Apple has refused to go on the record with any details about why it happened or, more importantly, what you and I could do to keep it from happening to us.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Suspicion is the Standard&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It's more common than you'd think.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;Using a gift card, even one from a major retailer, that's &lt;a href="https://appleinsider.com/articles/25/12/13/locked-out-how-a-gift-card-purchase-destroyed-an-apple-account"&gt;been tampered with&lt;/a&gt; without your knowledge&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://discussions.apple.com/thread/250521767"&gt;Filing a chargeback with your credit card company&lt;/a&gt; instead of letting Apple arbitrate a dispute over a purchase&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Making one too many &lt;a href="https://discussions.apple.com/thread/252625385"&gt;refund requests&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;&lt;a href="https://tidbits.com/2023/04/20/how-a-passcode-thief-can-lock-you-out-of-your-icloud-account-possibly-permanently/"&gt;Hijacked credentials&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;Using &lt;a href="https://support.apple.com/en-us/102651"&gt;Advanced Data Protection&lt;/a&gt; and losing access to your recovery credentials&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="6"&gt;An arbitrary decision by Apple with no explanation, which happens to &lt;a href="https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/776502"&gt;developer accounts&lt;/a&gt; as well&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;None of this requires Apple to be right. In 2023 a federal judge dismissed a class action over exactly this question, and the reasoning matters more than the outcome. Matthew Price ran multiple chargebacks on in-app purchases that didn't work, some of them after Apple's own support told him to take it up with his bank. Apple terminated his account, kept the $7.63 balance sitting in it, and cut him off from what he says was $24,590.05 in purchased content. Judge Haywood Gilliam &lt;a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/california/candce/4:2021cv02846/377043/64/"&gt;dismissed the case without leave to amend&lt;/a&gt;: "It is simply immaterial whether Plaintiff's multiple chargebacks were actually fraudulent or manipulative because even as alleged, Apple suspected that they were." Suspicion is the standard, and you agreed to it when you accepted the terms. The same terms say you "shall not sue or recover any damages from Apple" over a decision to terminate your access.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Actually Breaks&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Identity.&lt;/strong&gt; If your Apple Account &lt;em&gt;is&lt;/em&gt; an @icloud.com / @me.com / @mac.com address, closing the account kills the email address. Everything that uses it for password resets, two-factor, and billing now points at a dead mailbox.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;iCloud data.&lt;/strong&gt; Photos, Messages history, iCloud Drive, Notes, contacts, calendars, Safari data and Passwords all become inaccessible.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Account balance.&lt;/strong&gt; Any unused Apple Account credit is stranded, and a court has already said Apple has no obligation to give it back.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Purchased software and media.&lt;/strong&gt; Apps, books, films, music. The apps are what most people will miss; you can't update them and you can't reinstall them.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Hardware.&lt;/strong&gt; Your iPhone, iPad, Watch, AirPods, Apple TV, HomePod and Macs are effectively bricked. Not literally dead, but unable to sync, update, or function normally. Devices sign out of iMessage and can't sign back in.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="6"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Activation Lock.&lt;/strong&gt; A device tied to an account you no longer control can't be cleanly released, and erasing it does not clear the lock.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="7"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Subscriptions.&lt;/strong&gt; Apple One, iCloud+, Apple Music, App Store subscriptions and anything else billed through Apple.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="8"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Apple Developer ID.&lt;/strong&gt; Apps in review, TestFlight, certificates, provisioning profiles and App Store Connect, all gone.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="9"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Access to Apple's support channels.&lt;/strong&gt; The Secure File Transfer system Apple uses to collect your documentation requires an Apple Account sign-in, and so do most of the escalation paths Apple suggests. A locked account can't ask for help about being locked.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why Getting It Back Is Hard&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Apple won't tell you why your account was closed, reportedly out of fear that its fraud prevention methods will be reverse engineered. Frontline support staff don't have access to the reason either, so they can't find out on your behalf and they can't escalate your issue. Making a new account on hardware already linked to suspected fraud can earn you another ban for attempting to circumvent fraud prevention. I could find no documented path to export data from a closed account.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;How to Protect Yourself&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;Never buy an Apple Gift Card from anyone but Apple. If you get one as a gift, that's a harder call.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Never attempt a credit card chargeback on an Apple purchase of any kind.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Turn on &lt;a href="https://support.apple.com/en-us/120340"&gt;Stolen Device Protection&lt;/a&gt;, which means committing to 2FA, a passcode, Face or Touch ID, Significant Locations and Find My.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;Shield your device passcode in public, every single time, and make it a complex alphanumeric string instead of six digits.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;Set up a recovery contact and a recovery key.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="6"&gt;Some forum users keep a second Apple Account for media and purchases. I haven't tested it, but the logic holds.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="7"&gt;Do not use an @icloud.com address as your Apple Account.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="8"&gt;Own your email domain.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="9"&gt;Keep local, offline copies of everything.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="10"&gt;Run a data export on a schedule at &lt;a href="https://privacy.apple.com/"&gt;privacy.apple.com&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="11"&gt;Whenever possible, download software from the developer rather than the App Store.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tomorrow I'll post the apps and methods that let you keep using Mail, Calendar, Photos, Contacts and file storage without putting all of it inside one account Apple can close on suspicion.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=%20All%20Your%20Eggs%20in%20One%20Basket,%20The%20Apple%20Disaster%20Scenario" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>

1200w, https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBMXp5QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--c04e18d85b350f9bb90f9f5c5a3ecf52078c2dac/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lKYW5CbFp3WTZCa1ZVT2hSeVpYTnBlbVZmZEc5ZmJHbHRhWFJiQjJrQ0FBWnBBZ0FHT2dwellYWmxjbnNIT2d4eGRXRnNhWFI1YVZrNkNuTjBjbWx3VkE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoidmFyaWF0aW9uIn19--411f2a8ffe3d0e187cf33a269960b18282c19944/d0e27d49-8efb-4b58-81b3-0f7a4642826f.jpeg 1536w" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBMXp5QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--c04e18d85b350f9bb90f9f5c5a3ecf52078c2dac/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lKYW5CbFp3WTZCa1ZVT2hSeVpYTnBlbVZmZEc5ZmJHbHRhWFJiQjJrQ0lBTnBBaUFET2dwellYWmxjbnNIT2d4eGRXRnNhWFI1YVZrNkNuTjBjbWx3VkE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoidmFyaWF0aW9uIn19--6b540d5bfcfeca9a1dc6d345f6876757413a9f8d/d0e27d49-8efb-4b58-81b3-0f7a4642826f.jpeg" decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;TL;DR:&lt;/strong&gt; Four free iPhone apps that handle jobs you would normally do on your Mac: API Bot for testing endpoints, View Source Vibe for inspecting a suspicious link, Fiper for algorithm-free RSS, and Owl VIP for sender-level email notifications. Two earn a place on your phone. Fiper loses to NetNewsWire for anyone reading this blog, and Owl VIP charges a subscription for something iOS Focus Modes mostly do free. None has a native Mac app.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Every so often, something breaks and you are nowhere near your computer.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An endpoint starts returning 500 errors while you are sitting in a parking lot. Someone texts you a link and you want to see what trackers it loads before you trust it. You are waiting on one critical email, but your phone keeps buzzing about newsletters.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;These are Mac jobs. Your Mac is at home.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The obvious move is to reach for your phone. The obvious problem is that most "mobile versions of desktop tools" are just cramped, feature-starved versions of software you already own. The phone only wins when it does something your Mac cannot: being in your hand when you are away from your desk.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is the filter I applied to these four apps. Two pass it cleanly. Two do not.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;One technical note up front: none of these four has a native Mac app. Some will launch on an Apple silicon Mac, since iOS apps show up there by default unless the developer opts out, but what you get is a fixed, phone-shaped window that will not resize. Treat these as phone tools, full stop.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/api-bot/id1667144207"&gt;&lt;i&gt;&lt;strong&gt;API Bot&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/i&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you write or maintain APIs, Postman, Insomnia, and Bruno are likely glued to your workflow. They also assume you have a full keyboard and a large monitor. API Bot takes the opposite approach.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It is Postman built specifically for an iPhone screen. You can construct HTTP requests, set headers and query parameters, inspect JSON responses, and save requests as collections.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The use case is narrow, but real: you are away from your desk, an endpoint is behaving oddly, and you want to fire off a quick GET request to staging. It is not a replacement for Bruno on your desktop. It is the difference between diagnosing an outage immediately and waiting three hours until you get home.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It is free, and runs on iOS and iPadOS 13.0 or later. Confirm the permissions in the App Store yourself before installing, as there is little independent track record yet. As a focused utility for an away-from-the-desk problem, it earns its spot.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A competitior, &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/httpbot-api-http-client/id1232603544"&gt;HTTPBot: API &amp;amp; HTTP Client&lt;/a&gt; does what API Bot does and ships on &lt;a href="https://httpbot.io/"&gt;iOS, iPad, &lt;em&gt;and&lt;/em&gt; macOS&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/view-source-vibe/id6759335719"&gt;&lt;i&gt;&lt;strong&gt;View Source Vibe&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/i&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Viewing page source on a phone sounds like a gimmick. View Source Vibe turns it into a pocket web inspector.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Beyond raw HTML, it includes a Timeline view, OpenGraph social previews, a Cookie Privacy Lens, a Tracker Radar, Header Intelligence, and a Security Score Card. If someone sends you a link that feels off, this lets you inspect headers and tracking scripts on the spot before handing over your attention.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Also free, and it carries a "Data Not Collected" privacy label.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Here is the catch: the developer explicitly notes the app was "Built with Vibes (and Flutter)," indicating heavy use of AI-assisted coding. I have no issue with vibe-coding, but software that grades other sites on security while being built via LLM prompts demands healthy skepticism. Use its site analysis to satisfy your curiosity; do not rely on its Security Score Card as a formal audit.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.fiper.net/en/"&gt;&lt;i&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Fiper&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/i&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Fiper is an RSS reader designed to look like an Instagram feed rather than a list of text headlines.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It shows a chronological timeline without algorithmic sorting, auto-detects feeds simply by pasting a URL, and pulls in Bluesky, Mastodon, and Pixelfed accounts alongside traditional blogs. That is a thoughtful design position for people who find classic RSS intimidating.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It also has the weakest case for readers of this blog.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you are reading a Mac utility site, you have almost certainly solved RSS already. NetNewsWire is free, open source, and native on Mac and iOS. Reeder is beautiful. Feedly and Inoreader have a decade of infrastructure behind them.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Fiper is a pleasant, free app. Recommend it to family members who want off algorithmic feeds but will never set up NetNewsWire. For power users, there is no reason to switch.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/owl-vip-email-alerts/id6757348256"&gt;&lt;i&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Owl VIP Email Alerts&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/i&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Owl VIP attempts to fix phone notifications at the sender level.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It hooks into Gmail to give you global notification toggles (VIP-only, All, or None), custom quiet hours, and per-sender audio alerts from a library of 80+ sounds. Being able to triage who emailed you by ear without picking up your phone is a clever idea.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The problem is the business model and the built-in alternatives.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The app is free to download, but requires a paid subscription to connect a Gmail account. Nearly everything it does can be built for free using Gmail's native filters combined with iOS Focus Modes. Paying a recurring subscription strictly for custom notification sounds is a hard sell.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It also only works with Gmail. Spend twenty minutes configuring Focus Modes first.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;My Take&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/api-bot/id1667144207"&gt;&lt;em&gt;API Bot&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/a&gt; is an easy download if you deal with APIs and ever need to test an endpoint on the go.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/view-source-vibe/id6759335719"&gt;&lt;em&gt;View Source Vibe&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/a&gt; answers a specific question when inspecting suspicious links, provided you treat its security scores as informational.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.fiper.net/en/"&gt;&lt;em&gt;Fiper&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/a&gt; is a great recommendation for non-technical friends, but skip it if you already run NetNewsWire or Reeder.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/owl-vip-email-alerts/id6757348256"&gt;&lt;em&gt;Owl VIP Email Alerts&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/a&gt; has a clever audio trick, but iOS Focus Modes cover most of its feature set without a subscription.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Three of these four apps have virtually no independent review track record. That is normal for early indie software, but it means you are the test case.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;Unless otherwise noted, the alternate apps mentioned above are based on research and not individual testing.&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=When%20You%20Need%20a%20Mac,%20But%20All%20You%20Have%20is%20a%20Phone%20-%20The%20Verdict%20on%20Four%20Free%20Alternatives%20to%20Leaving%20Work%20Undone" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>

2197w" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBNzN3QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--cfec00d6195276204152f593930f33fb9a9c6cd3/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJZ0Eya0NJQU02Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--8cebb1c2983a7e4106444e274de6ebedc86813b1/CleanShot%202026-08-01%20at%2013.27.19.jpg" decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;TL;DR:&lt;/strong&gt; RAD Weather pulls forecasts from four services and shows you where they disagree instead of averaging the disagreement away. Free, with RAD Ultra at $1.99 a month, $19.99 a year, or $99.99 once, plus a MultiPass tier at $2.99 monthly or $29.99 annual. The Mac build is a real Mac app, the subscription is justified by per-forecast data costs, and there is no radar. RAD TV shipped in 7.6.7 and an Apple TV version is announced.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;RAD Weather's Unique Feature&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Years of obsessive cycling naturally paired with years of obsessive weather forecast following. Although none of us can do anything about the weather (except to move to a new city), I felt compelled to track temperature, wind speed and rain forecasts several times a day whenever I had a big ride scheduled. I collected weather apps and went into mourning when Dark Sky ceased to exist.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Most weather apps are someone's best guess, presented as a fact. Someone, or some algorithm, took several disagreeing weather services, picked one and discarded the rest. &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/rad-weather-honest-forecast/id6758575355"&gt;RAD Weather&lt;/a&gt; doesn't discard anything, and that's the product.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What R.A.D. Cortex Is Doing Under the Hood&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The engine has a name now, R.A.D. Cortex, and its job is to pull forecasts from the National Weather Service, Open-Meteo, Environment and Climate Change Canada, and Apple WeatherKit, then compare them. Where the models converge, you get a high confidence rating. Where they split, the app shows you the spread instead of hiding it behind an average. The developer added lead-time-aware weighting in an earlier release, so regional high-resolution models carry more weight for the next few hours while ECMWF gets priority for the extended outlook. That's a reasonable thing to do, and it's the kind of decision most weather apps make silently, if they make it at all.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Five Things That Matter in the Mac Version&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;It's a real Mac app. Many weather apps just port their iPad version to Apple silicon and call it a day. CARROT Weather has a standalone Mac app, but it hasn't been updated since 2023. With RAD Weather, you also get Mac widgets, a menu bar item, and iCloud sync with the iPhone and Watch versions. Requires macOS 15.0 or later.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;The multi-source view is the killer feature. Detail cards break out temperature, wind, precipitation, UV, pressure, humidity, visibility, dew point, pollen, air quality and convective risk, and the confidence deep-dive shows you which models fed the number. It's my favorite part of the app and I never stop fiddling with it.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;RAD Atlas is an interactive 3D globe with live conditions, which sounds like a toy and mostly is, but it's a fast way to check what's happening somewhere you care about without typing a city name.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;Brutality Levels adjust the tone of the written briefings across five settings, from professional to unhinged. Similar to CARROT, which is funny, RAD Weather is also funny. Since humor is subjective, I'm not making a call there. If you want a weather app that doesn't talk to you, turn it to professional and it stops.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;The privacy declaration is clean. Rozzi Labs declares no data collected beyond location, not linked to your identity, used only to fetch a forecast, with no tracking or analytics. That's about as good as a networked weather app gets.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What the Subscription Pays For&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;RAD Weather is free. RAD Ultra is $1.99 a month, $19.99 a year, or $99.99 once, and Ultra is what unlocks the Atlas globe, the extra saved locations, the Savage and Unhinged tone settings, full detail cards and advanced notifications. There's also RAD MultiPass at $2.99 a month or $29.99 a year, which extends across the other Rozzi Labs apps and the radweather.cloud web service.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;No one likes an unjustified subscription. I've done my best recently to avoid writing about subscription apps altogether. Weather prediction apps are the exception. Every forecast this app pulls costs the developer money, and he's pulling from four services instead of one; widget and Watch complication refreshes multiply that cost across every user, every day, forever. A one-time purchase doesn't fund a bill that arrives monthly for the life of the app. The developer of CARROT Weather has been making the same argument for years, and he's right.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The whole high-end category runs this way. CARROT Weather is free to download with Premium at $4.99 a month or $19.99 a year and Premium Ultra at $9.99 a month or $39.99 a year. &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/mercury-weather/id1621800675"&gt;Mercury Weather&lt;/a&gt; is free with a subscription at $2.99 a month or $14.99 a year. &lt;a href="https://helloweather.com/"&gt;Hello Weather&lt;/a&gt; limits you to a single forecaster and no widgets until you subscribe. Against all that, RAD Weather is one of only two apps here that will sell you a permanent copy. RAD Ultra Lifetime is $99.99, which works out to five years of the annual subscription; Mercury's lifetime is $59.99, or four years of its annual. Neither is a bargain on day one. CARROT has no lifetime tier at any price, which is the part I mind.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Current Shortcomings&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;RAD Weather doesn't currently offer radar maps, so if that's how you make decisions during rough times, you'll need something else. There are other weather apps with a long and proven track record. Its App Store rating is high, but the number of ratings behind it is still small enough that I wouldn't lean on it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Other Weather Apps&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The alternatives, briefly. &lt;strong&gt;CARROT Weather&lt;/strong&gt;, to which I have subscribed for years, is the incumbent in personality weather and has the better radar and map layer story; note that &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/carrot-weather/id993487541?mt=12"&gt;the standalone Mac app&lt;/a&gt; is $14.99 and hasn't been updated since May 2023, so on the Mac you want the iPhone and iPad version instead. &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/mercury-weather/id1621800675"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Mercury Weather&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt;, another app I've used in the past, is the choice if you want calm and legible rather than loud. &lt;strong&gt;Apple Weather&lt;/strong&gt; is free, built in, and fine for the basics. &lt;a href="https://github.com/inderdhir/DatWeatherDoe"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;DatWeatherDoe&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt; is free, open source under Apache 2.0, installs with &lt;code&gt;brew install --cask datweatherdoe&lt;/code&gt;, and puts conditions in your menu bar; you supply your own WeatherAPI key.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Unless otherwise noted, the alternate apps mentioned above are based on research and not individual testing.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Is It for You?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Yes, if you want accuracy and detail from a weather app and you're willing to pay for it. The multiplatform coverage helps too, especially with the recently released full screen RAD TV mode for the Mac and an Apple TV app on the way.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;No, if you want radar, or your needs are minimal. For design nerds, the faux terminal presentation may be off-putting. Not being a design nerd, I'm fine with it.&lt;/p&gt;

1200w, https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBNHZ2QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--35fbc9cd9c3b399790d01d667298c86d4ef3cf23/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFKQUJta0NRQVk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--9632f1ea6e4e0a3e5199810d4639e5789e3b076c/orbit.jpg 2012w" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBNHZ2QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--35fbc9cd9c3b399790d01d667298c86d4ef3cf23/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJZ0Eya0NJQU02Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--8cebb1c2983a7e4106444e274de6ebedc86813b1/orbit.jpg" alt="The interface for Orbit, a native Mac Gmail app." decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;TL;DR:&lt;/strong&gt; Orbit runs each of your Google accounts in its own isolated WebKit session inside one native Mac window, for $89 one time instead of the $50 to $200 a year the alternatives want. It exists because you can de-Google yourself but you can't de-Google your father. The catch is that it only works as long as Google keeps letting Mac apps sign in, and passkey-only and Advanced Protection accounts already can't.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;The Google Accounts I Didn't Ask For&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;My opinion of big tech companies has hardened over the years. Their business models turned into anti-privacy juggernauts, so I started pulling away from them. In January 2025, after using Gmail for twenty years, I downloaded my entire archive, deleted every message off their servers and moved to Fastmail. Drive went to Koofr. Search went to Kagi. Gemini got replaced by ChatGPT. I left the empty account open since it linked me to a lot of legacy logins and contacts.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Then, nine months later, I became responsible for managing the affairs of my elderly father, something that commonly happens to people in my age group. Dad's life ran through multiple Gmail accounts, personal and professional: his doctors, his investments and the guy who cuts his grass all reached him through Google, the company I had worked so hard to get away from. I couldn't ask an 80-year-old man to move house on the internet. I had to log back in.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That's the part nobody warns you about. You can de-Google yourself in a weekend if you're stubborn. You can't de-Google somebody else, and the account that drags you back in was never yours to begin with.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Browsers do this badly on purpose. Google's account switcher runs every account you sign into through a single browser session, so a security re-check on one can sign you out of all of them at once, and the account you're currently "in" is a state you have to remember rather than see. Everybody who lives this way eventually has the moment where they send, or nearly send, a message from the wrong account. Sometimes that's an embarrassment. Sometimes it's worse.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The fix is an app, and the one I recommend is &lt;a href="https://orbitformac.com/"&gt;Orbit&lt;/a&gt; from Andrew Kwak at Dearnode. It's a one-time purchase of $89. That's a steep number to look at once, and cheaper than every competitor that charges $50 a year and up.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Each account gets its own sealed WebKit session, with its own cookies and its own sign-in, so signing into one never signs you out of another. ⌘1 through ⌘9 switch between them, all preloaded, with unread badges per account. Inside each one is the real Gmail, not a rebuild through the API, so your labels, filters and keyboard shortcuts are the ones you already have. Calendar, Drive and Meet open in the right account too. I have three accounts in mine.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why I picked Orbit&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Orbit is designed around privacy. It doesn't route your mail through a server it owns. There is no Orbit account to maintain. Analytics are turned off by default. It doesn't phone home, and if Dearnode vanished tomorrow, Orbit would keep working until Google changes something on their end.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Because Dearnode has no servers to maintain, the one-time price is sustainable. &lt;a href="https://www.kiwiforgmail.com/"&gt;Kiwi&lt;/a&gt;, the app I used for years with Gmail, committed what I consider an unpardonable sin earlier this year when it stopped honoring lifetime licenses it had already sold and moved every customer to $60 a year. It's not the only casualty in this category: &lt;a href="https://efficient.app/apps/sidekick"&gt;Sidekick&lt;/a&gt; was absorbed by Perplexity and shut down in 2025, and &lt;a href="https://tidbits.com/2021/06/08/mailplane-stops-selling-licenses/"&gt;Mailplane&lt;/a&gt; stopped selling licenses in 2021.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Orbit is written in Swift and runs on WebKit. It weighs 9.9 MB on my system, a far cry from the Electron build behind Shift.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why it might not work for you&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;To his credit, Orbit's developer publishes the warnings himself rather than waiting for a reviewer to find them:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;Sign-in is per-Mac. Three machines means three sign-ins, and there's no cross-device sync.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Accounts using passkey-only sign-in or Google's Advanced Protection Program can't sign in at all, due to a WebKit limitation.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;It's Apple silicon and macOS 14 or later. No Intel.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;It's not on the Mac App Store, because the sandbox would break the per-account isolation the whole app exists for.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;And one risk that isn't Kwak's fault and isn't in his power to fix. Orbit works because Google lets a Mac app sign in and render Gmail. Google can withdraw that. It has before: Mailplane stopped selling licenses in 2021 when Google started blocking embedded browsers at the sign-in page, and Mailplane was the same idea as Orbit, Gmail's web interface in a Mac shell. The accounts Orbit can't sign in today, the passkey-only and Advanced Protection ones, are that same door already partly closed.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Kwak has built the parts he controls to fail quietly. If Google reshuffles Gmail's page, an unread badge goes stale instead of your mail breaking, because the mail was never his code. That's the right way to build this. It just doesn't help with the failure that matters, which is Google deciding one morning that apps like this don't get in anymore.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Others&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Every alternative here costs you something. Some want a subscription, some run on a browser engine you didn't ask for, and the free ones make you give up the switching and the badges.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://mimestream.com/pricing/"&gt;Mimestream&lt;/a&gt; is well liked, and it's also $50 a year.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://shift.com/pricing/"&gt;Shift&lt;/a&gt; is $200 a year and it's Electron. There's a free tier some people will find suitable.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.kiwiforgmail.com/"&gt;Kiwi for Gmail&lt;/a&gt; was my daily driver for years and it worked. Their decision to stop honoring lifetime licenses blunts any regard I once had for them.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://ferdium.org/"&gt;Ferdium&lt;/a&gt; is free and open source. Community-built, Electron, and it will hold multiple instances of the same service. I've run it myself. Free is free.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://support.apple.com/guide/safari/create-profiles-ibrwf3a9e7d6/mac"&gt;Safari profiles&lt;/a&gt; are already on your Mac, and I've used them for this. Separate cookies and separate sign-ins per profile, no purchase, no keyboard switching, no unread badges. If you have two accounts, try this before you spend anything.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I haven't personally tested Mimestream or Shift and this information comes from their websites.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Who should buy this&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Writing about a Google adjacent app doesn't mean I've reconsidered anything. Fastmail, Koofr and Kagi are still where I manage my own life. But I couldn't de-Google on my father's behalf. Pretending otherwise would have cost him his pharmacy, his insurance and his bank. His accounts aren't a preference, they're an obligation, and the software worth paying for is the software that makes an obligation easiest to manage.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you're carrying three or more Google accounts you didn't choose, you switch between them all day, and you've had the wrong-sender scare, $89 once is a fair price for never having that thought again. There's a 14-day trial that doesn't ask for a card and a 30-day refund window, so trying it costs you an afternoon.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you have two accounts, Safari profiles are free. If you want a real native mail client and a merged inbox, Mimestream is the app and the subscription is the tax. And if you run Advanced Protection, Orbit can't sign you in at all, which puts it out of reach for exactly the people its architecture was built to appeal to.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Using%20Orbit%20to%20manage%20the%20Google%20accounts%20I%20didn" t want style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>

decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;TL;DR:&lt;/strong&gt; Blankie is a free, open-source ambient sound mixer for Mac, iPhone, iPad and CarPlay; no ads, IAPs, or subscriptions. 24 mixable sounds, saved presets, custom audio import, menu bar control. Stacked against Noizio, Dark Noise, myNoise, and Endel, all of which charge something for depth or convenience Blankie gives away for free.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I'm not usually one to complain about app pricing, but I make an exception when it feels like someone is misrepresenting the complexity of something simple to justify a monetization strategy. Ambient sound apps, at their core, are well-organized loop players, and nothing about them justifies subscriptions, tiered unlocks, and $50 lifetime passes. You get rain, waves, white noise and a coffee shop hum with variations. That's the whole package.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Enter &lt;a href="https://blankie.rest/"&gt;Blankie&lt;/a&gt;, a free and open-source ambient sound mixer from developer Cody Bromley that gives you everything you need without insulting your intelligence or your wallet. It also respects your privacy by not collecting any data. It's inspired by &lt;a href="https://github.com/rafaelmardojai/blanket"&gt;Blanket&lt;/a&gt;, a Linux app in the same category. Blankie avoids ads, IAPs, subscription tiers and paywalls. It's just free, forever. Better yet, it works on your Mac, your phone, your iPad and your car.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;How it works&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;With Blankie, it's easy to construct custom loops and recall them at will. You get 24 sound elements to experiment with, including several added in the most recent updates: rain, storms, wind, ocean waves, a running stream, birds, forest, crickets, a train, boat, airplane, city hum, coffee shop, fireplace, fan, laundry room, plus a few music-adjacent layers (piano, lo-fi beats, guitar, ambient synth) and the full noise family (white, pink, green, brown).&lt;/p&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/blankie/id6740096581"&gt;App Store link&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The features that matter&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;Per-sound volume control: every layer has its own slider on top of a master volume, so you're not stuck with someone else's idea of "coffee shop" balance.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Saved presets: build a mix once for deep work, another for sleep, and switch between them instead of re-tuning sliders every time.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Bring your own audio: you can import your own sounds or voice notes, and Blankie loudness-matches them automatically so nothing jumps out of the mix. I experimented with the sound of my own box fan and it worked!&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;Sleep timer with fade-out: it winds down and stops instead of just cutting off, which matters more than it sounds like it should at 11pm.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;Menu bar control: as of version 2.0 there's a menu bar popover for quick mix and timer changes, plus an option to hide the Dock icon entirely, both added directly in response to user feedback on the App Store.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Do you need an app for this?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;One of the under-publicized features available in macOS Accessibility settings is a control for background sounds. You can get a flat layer of white noise without installing anything. If that does the trick to drown out your office mate's Zoom calls, then you're golden. If you want actual combinations you can control, layering rain with a fireplace, mixing to your own balance, saving distinct presets, and importing your own recordings, Apple's built-in version doesn't do any of that.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The apps I complained about&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I've tried Noizio and Endel. They work, but they cost more than they're worth.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/noizio-calm-meditate-sleep/id928871589?mt=12"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Noizio&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt; ($9.99 one-time, Mac App Store, also on Setapp) has 40 sounds behind the paid tier versus 5 free, and I covered it here previously; it's the closest direct comparison and the app several Blankie reviewers say they're switching from.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.macrumors.com/2023/04/03/dark-noise-switches-to-subscription-pricing/"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Dark Noise&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt; now runs $2.99/month or $19.99/year for full access after moving off its original one-time-purchase model in 2023, with a free tier limited to eight sounds; there's still a $49.99 lifetime option for people who want to opt out of the subscription entirely.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/mynoise-focus-relax-sleep/id1523675125"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;myNoise&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt; is free to download with a $19.99 in-app purchase ("Full Access") that unlocks its full 300+-soundscape library; it's a much deeper catalog aimed partly at tinnitus masking and therapeutic use, not just background focus noise.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.autonomous.ai/ourblog/endel-app-review"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Endel&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt;  If you want the adaptive end of this category, runs $19.99/month or roughly $89.99/year (with a ~$249 lifetime option), and generates sound algorithmically rather than letting you hand-build a mix; different product, This may be the most over-priced app I've even seen.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Unless otherwise noted, the alternate apps mentioned above are based on research and not individual testing.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Bottom Line&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Use Blankie if you want a free, privacy-respecting sound mixer that doesn't hold features hostage behind a subscription, and you're fine with a smaller sound library (24) than the subscription apps offer in exchange for owning the whole thing outright. If you own something else already or you just really need hundreds of soundscapes and don't mind paying, go with myNoise.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Blankie,%20A%20Free%20and%20Open%20Source%20Ambient%20Sound%20Mixer%20is%20a%20Breath%20of%20Fresh%20Air,%20Right%20in%20Your%20Ear" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>
    <summary>TL;DR: Blankie is a free, open-source ambient sound mixer for Mac, iPhone, iPad and CarPlay; no ads, IAPs, or subscriptions. 24 mixable sounds, saved presets, custom audio import, menu bar control. Stacked against Noizio, Dark Noise, myNoise, and Endel, all of which charge something for depth or convenience Blankie gives away...</summary>

decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Mac users tend to be nostalgic about the hardware and software they used in their earliest exposure to tech. That doesn't mean anyone wants to try to get real work done on a late-90s PowerPC Mac clone, or go back to 14-inch monitors. People just enjoy being reminded how far we've come, and pretend there was once a time when everything "just worked." (It didn't. I was there.)&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;German developer Maik Klotz created a free app, &lt;a href="https://myretromac.app/"&gt;RetroMac&lt;/a&gt;, that turns your current Mac into a version of the Wayback Machine. It doesn't touch your system. It paints. A Metal shader sits on top of whatever's already rendering: CRT curvature, scanlines, VHS tracking noise. It can also swap your dock, wallpaper, boot screen, and cursor set for a specific era's look: Windows 98, Windows XP, System 6, Mac OS 9, Mac OS X Aqua, Snow Leopard, BeOS, NeXTSTEP. If all that lickable tech scares you, you go back to boring just by quitting RetroMac.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;How Much Time Travel Do You Want?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;Get a little or a lot. RetroMac's modular design combines your choice of elements to build a look you're comfortable with. There are toggles for shader, theme, dock, Retro TV, and live wallpaper. Play around with everything but the one window you want your boss to see if he wanders by. That one you can keep sharp.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Pick a window, or a display. The shader works on a single window, but it's more fun to turn your secondary display into a period piece. Fire up an old game on YouTube and let it run while your co-workers gather round.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Themes go deep. You get matching cursors, icon sets, boot splashes, and actual .saver modules (Flying Toasters, Flurry, 3D Pipes) in every shipped theme. RetroMac is more than a wallpaper shuffle with a dock overlay.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;Retro TV is its own feature. Play a variety of video streams in a CRT-framed window, or use it in your next Zoom meeting (or Teams, or Meet) if your clients and co-workers have a sense of humor.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;It's easy to go back to normal. Health Check plus one-click restore for wallpaper, dock, and menu bar. Free to use, with a one-time €8.88 Pro upgrade for extra shader presets, custom presets, and the webcam shader. No subscription, no account, no telemetry.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Yeah, But Why?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Sometimes an app is just fun, and this falls into that category, but there are a few semi-practical uses too:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;Screen recording&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Retro gaming&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Showcase setups&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;Music videos&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Do You Really Need an App for This?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Depends what you're actually nostalgic for.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/this-mac-app-can-turn-every-window-into-a-crt-fever-dream-or-a-nostalgic-game-boy/"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Glaze&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt; ($9.99 one-time) is the closest direct competitor: a live GPU-shader overlay for your whole Mac with 50+ looks, including CRT, VHS, Game Boy, comic-book, and oil-painting filters. It skips the classic-OS theme replication entirely and focuses on the shader layer, so if you just want the tube-TV look on a normal desktop without the Windows 98 cosplay, it's narrower and cheaper.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.macworld.com/article/2873012/retrostrip-review.html"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;retroStrip&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt; is the odd one out: not a shader app at all, but a modern recreation of the classic Mac OS Control Strip, the little floating bar of one-click controls from System 7.1 onward. The base app is free (retroStrip LE); additional icon theme packs are $2 each or $5 for all three. If what you actually miss is the Control Strip specifically, this is a tighter, single-purpose tool than RetroMac's dock feature.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://github.com/dirkwhoffmann/RetroVisor"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;RetroVisor&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt; is free and open source, a ScreenCaptureKit-and-Metal shader overlay clearly modeled on Windows' ShaderGlass. It runs in a floating window rather than full screen and has none of RetroMac's theme, dock, or Retro TV features. Good pick if all you want is the CRT glass effect and you don't want to pay anything.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Two flags on that. First, these three comparisons are based on research, not testing; I haven't installed any of them myself. Second, that actually cuts in RetroMac's favor: you'd have to install and configure all three to come close to what one app does by itself.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Obligatory War Story&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Apple released its last CRT-equipped computer in 2003 and discontinued it three years later.. Targeted at the education market, the eMac came in one color: white. It lacked the iMac's convenient carrying handle and weighed in at over 50 pounds, looking for all the world like the front end of the space shuttle viewed from behind. Most of them wouldn't run any version of OS X beyond Tiger. My employer, a rural school district in North Carolina, bought them by the thousands. I was the "Mac guy," so I spent months of my life unboxing eMacs for computer labs and placing them in every K-5 classroom in the district. It gave me PTSD, and to this day I can't look at a 17-inch CRT (or Tiger) without flinching.&lt;/p&gt;
